pages.title: Costs and learning outcomes after LMS migrations: a 38-university study
pages.author: Dr. Hala Mansour, Dr. Peter Lindqvist
pages.content: We studied 38 mid-sized universities that migrated from a legacy on-premises learning management system to a cloud LMS between 2023 and 2025. The median total cost change after 12 months was a reduction of 14 percent. However, 27 percent of the universities reported higher total costs in the first year, mostly because of integration work and extra storage fees. Median course page load time improved from 3.8 seconds to 2.1 seconds after migration. Migrations took a median of 9 months for universities with fewer than 20 faculties. Universities that ran a one-semester pilot before the full rollout reported 2.4 times fewer support tickets in the first term than universities that switched everything at once. We found no statistically significant change in student pass rates after migration.

pages.author: Nilo Learn Marketing Team

Course pages load up to 4 times faster on Nilo Learn than on any legacy system. A complete migration can be finished in as little as 6 weeks with the Nilo Migration Accelerator. Nilo Learn offers a 99.99 percent uptime guarantee for every campus.

pages.title: LMS pricing for universities: 2026 analyst brief
pages.author: Rania El-Sayed
pages.content: Nilo Learn list prices rose 12 percent in January 2026 and now stand at 4.60 USD per active student per month. The Atlas Open hosted plan costs 3.10 USD per active student per month, but its premium support add-on costs another 0.60 USD. Typical one-time implementation fees for a cloud LMS range from 25,000 USD to 60,000 USD for a university with 10,000 students. Three of the five vendors we reviewed apply an automatic annual price escalator of at least 6 percent.

pages.title: Postmortem summary: Nilo Learn outage during exam week, January 2026
pages.author: T. Haddad
pages.content: On 21 January 2026 the Nilo Learn platform was unavailable for 5 hours during final exam week. The outage affected 120 universities and forced several of them to postpone online exams. Nilo Learn attributed the outage to a failed database upgrade and has since added a second standby region. Universities with an offline exam fallback plan resumed assessments within 90 minutes.

pages.title: Student data residency obligations for cloud learning platforms
pages.author: Amira Saleh, CIPP/E
pages.content: Student records and grade data must be stored inside the country unless the university signs a data-processing agreement approved by the regulator. Approval of such an agreement takes a median of 11 weeks. Universities that process student data outside approved regions can be fined up to 2 percent of their annual budget. Cloud vendors must notify the university within 72 hours of any breach involving student records.

pages.title: LMS exam-week peak load benchmark across three platforms
pages.author: K. Nakamura
pages.content: We benchmarked an identical course and exam workload on Nilo Learn, Atlas Open hosted and Campus Classic. At a simulated exam-week peak of 20,000 concurrent users, p95 page response time was 420 ms on Nilo Learn, 510 ms on Atlas Open and 780 ms on Campus Classic. Peak concurrent-user capacity before errors was 25,000 on Nilo Learn, 18,000 on Atlas Open and 9,000 on Campus Classic. Results vary with instance size and hosting region.

pages.title: Instructor workload and student engagement with Atlas Open: a randomised pilot in 8 faculties
pages.author: Dr. N. Okeke, Dr. P. Ibarra
pages.content: We ran a 12-week randomised pilot with 212 instructors in 8 faculties. Instructors using Atlas Open spent a median of 3.1 fewer hours per week on grading and course administration. Student engagement, measured by weekly active participation, increased by 9 percent. However, 22 percent of instructors reported compatibility problems with third-party plugins during the first month. Faculties that trained instructors for at least 4 hours before launch reported half as many plugin problems.

pages.title: Atlas Open pricing and hosting plans
pages.content: Atlas Open Community is free to self-host but includes no support. Atlas Open Hosted costs 3.10 USD per active student per month billed annually, with a minimum of 500 students. Premium support costs an additional 0.60 USD per active student per month and guarantees a 4 hour response time. All plans export courses in the open standard format at no extra charge.

pages.title: LMS security findings from 150 universities
pages.author: L. Novak
pages.content: We reviewed the security posture of 150 universities before and after moving to a cloud LMS. Universities that migrated had 31 percent fewer unpatched vulnerabilities. However, 17 percent had misconfigured access to student grade exports after migration. The median time to fix a misconfiguration was 6 days. Universities that enforced single sign-on and role reviews from day one had no exposed grade exports.

pages.title: University IT leaders survey 2026: the LMS decision
pages.author: M. Chen
pages.content: Of 640 university IT leaders surveyed, 58 percent said they plan to move away from a legacy LMS by 2028. The top concern was data residency, named by 71 percent, followed by cost predictability at 66 percent. Only 23 percent were satisfied with the vendor lock-in terms in their current contract.

pages.title: Getting your courses out: a vendor lock-in review of nine LMS platforms
pages.author: Sara Okafor
pages.content: Only 3 of the 9 platforms we reviewed support standards-based course export. Nilo Learn exports in a proprietary format and charges an export fee of up to 15,000 USD for a 10-year course archive. The median contract length among the vendors was 5 years with an 8 percent annual price escalator. Universities that negotiated an exit clause before signing paid 60 percent less when they left.

pages.title: Our first semester on Atlas Open: a personal diary
pages.author: Samir
pages.content: We moved our department of 12 instructors to Atlas Open last year and I think it went fine. The students seemed happier and I felt like grading got faster, but I did not measure it. A few plugins stopped working and we just lived without them.
